title: Humanoid classroom robots show potential as teaching assistants, not teacher replacements
excerpt: A New York school district made global headlines this week for plans to trial a humanoid robot named "Sally" in high school classrooms.
content_html:
A New York school district made global headlines this week for plans to trial a humanoid robot named "Sally" in high school classrooms.

Sally has lifelike silicone skin, long brown hair and the ability to move her arms, head and face while seated. According to the manufacturer, she uses "natural conversation, facial expressions and real-time interaction."

She is programmed to be a stationary classroom teaching assistant and would work as a chatbot to answer student and teacher questions. She would also be available to students 24/7 as a digital avatar online.

Following concerns about student privacy, data storage and tracking, the project has been paused.

But how far away are we from having humanlike robots or AI-enhanced avatars as routine features of school classrooms?

Robots are not new to classrooms

Sally is not the first robot to be proposed for classrooms.

Nonhumanlike robots (such as "Nao") have been trialed in classrooms before. For example, they have been used to help students learn languages in Japan, South Korea, Europe and East Asia. They have also been used in technology classes to teach skills such as coding.

Tools such as Alexa, which responds to voice commands, have also been trialed in primary classrooms in New Zealand. Here, results varied by age. Younger children had difficulty asking questions in the right format to get the answers they were seeking. Older students tested the limits of the technology, exploring social interactions such as joke-telling or seeking unusual responses.

Teachers are also increasingly turning to generative AI for administrative tasks to save time, while chatbots are now regularly used in schools in Australia. For example, South Australia and New South Wales have introduced their own generative AI tools for students and teachers.

This growing day-to-day familiarity is likely to lower the barrier to more advanced, humanlike technologies entering classrooms.

Here to help

Research on AI-based avatars (which chat like a human but exist only online) found they can have a positive effect on learning.

They can provide on-demand academic support by individualizing learning. For example, they can patiently go over a math problem step by step.

They can also help with self-regulation by teaching strategies and repeatedly encouraging students to apply them over time. For example, "Before you start this equation, take a deep breath."

Students have also reported experiencing less pressure and anxiety when interacting with AI tutors, which are often perceived as less judgmental than teachers.

But we still need real teachers

A robot can simulate warmth, deliver curriculum flawlessly and never get tired or need a break.

However, evidence indicates these technologies are most effective when used alongside teachers, rather than replacing them.

For example, a 2026 meta-analysis of 146 studies found that social robots (robots that have a physical presence in the classroom) used to teach cognitive skills could improve learning outcomes, especially when they could personalize responses. But this was only when a teacher was present.

Robots used as teacher substitutes, however, could not manage the complexity of classroom content, respond to spontaneous student behavior or handle unforeseen occurrences.

Research also tells us children and young people learn best when they are engaged not just cognitively but also with other people.

They need interactions that build trust and instill confidence that they are seen, known and cared about by their teachers and peers in human ways that make sense to all involved.

Data, privacy and beyond

There are safety concerns with this technology as well.

As a robot interacts with a child, the interaction is recorded. This allows the robot to provide targeted and personalized responses. When programmed with generative AI, the data may be accumulated and used to inform future interactions with other students.

But this creates risks around data privacy, storage and tracking.

It also leads to other questions about who programs and controls the robots, and to what end. What happens if the program or data is hacked?

Can children learn empathy from a robot?

Teachers are in a position of significant trust, in charge of vulnerable children and young people. There are legislative frameworks and teacher registration boards that regulate teachers' professional behavior, but they do not extend to robots.

Teachers are obliged to identify, protect and foster students' best interests. This requires them to make nuanced judgments about individual learning needs, behavior and well-being.

This can be difficult to capture in fixed rules, instructions or robot programming.

As researchers have noted, this also raises concerns about children's development if they are interacting with simulated rather than genuine care and empathy.

What's next?

We are not going to have humanlike robots in classrooms tomorrow. But the developments out of New York show how they might be a serious option for the future—particularly amid ongoing concerns about teacher shortages and workloads.

If we are going to move further in this direction, there are tough questions to answer. We will need teachers present to make sure robots are used in ways that help and protect students as they interact and learn.

content_html_zh:
纽约一个学区本周因计划在高中教室试用名为“莎莉”的人形机器人而成为全球头条新闻。

莎莉拥有栩栩如生的硅胶皮肤、棕色长发，并且能够在坐着时移动手臂、头部和面部。 据制造商称，她使用“自然的对话、面部表情和实时互动”。

她被编程为固定课堂助教，并作为聊天机器人回答学生和老师的问题。 她还可以作为在线数字化身为学生提供 24/7 全天候服务。

由于担心学生隐私、数据存储和跟踪，该项目已暂停。

但是，我们离类人机器人或人工智能增强化身成为学校教室的常规功能还有多远呢？

机器人对于课堂来说并不陌生

莎莉并不是第一个被提议用于教室的机器人。

非人形机器人（例如“Nao”）之前曾在教室中进行过试用。 例如，它们已被用来帮助学生学习日本、韩国、欧洲和东亚的语言。 它们还被用于技术课程中教授编码等技能。

Alexa 等响应语音命令的工具也已在新西兰的小学教室进行了试用。 在这里，结果因年龄而异。 年幼的孩子很难以正确的方式提出问题来获得他们想要的答案。 年长的学生测试了技术的极限，探索社交互动，例如讲笑话或寻求不寻常的反应。

教师也越来越多地使用生成式人工智能来执行管理任务，以节省时间，而聊天机器人现在在澳大利亚的学校中经常使用。 例如，南澳大利亚和新南威尔士州为学生和教师推出了自己的生成式人工智能工具。

这种日益增长的日常熟悉度可能会降低更先进的、类人技术进入课堂的障碍。

在这里提供帮助

对基于人工智能的化身（像人类一样聊天，但仅存在于网上）的研究发现，它们可以对学习产生积极影响。

他们可以通过个性化学习提供按需学术支持。 例如，他们可以耐心地一步一步地解决数学问题。

他们还可以通过教授策略并反复鼓励学生长期应用这些策略来帮助自我调节。 例如，“在开始这个方程式之前，请深呼吸。”

学生们还表示，在与人工智能导师互动时，他们感受到的压力和焦虑减轻了，因为人工智能导师通常被认为比老师更少评判。

但我们仍然需要真正的老师

机器人可以模拟温暖，完美地教授课程，并且永远不会感到疲倦或需要休息。

然而，有证据表明，这些技术在与教师一起使用时最有效，而不是取代他们。

例如，2026 年对 146 项研究进行的荟萃分析发现，用于教授认知技能的社交机器人（实际存在于教室中的机器人）可以改善学习成果，特别是当它们可以个性化响应时。 但这只是在有老师在场的情况下发生的。

然而，用作教师替代品的机器人无法管理课堂内容的复杂性，无法响应学生的自发行为或处理不可预见的事件。

研究还告诉我们，儿童和年轻人不仅在认知上而且与其他人交往时学得最好。

他们需要通过互动来建立信任并灌输信心，让他们相信自己被老师和同龄人以对所有参与者都有意义的人性化方式看待、了解和关心。

数据、隐私及其他

这项技术也存在安全问题。

当机器人与孩子互动时，互动会被记录下来。 这使得机器人能够提供有针对性的个性化响应。 当使用生成式人工智能进行编程时，数据可以被积累并用于为未来与其他学生的互动提供信息。

但这会带来数据隐私、存储和跟踪方面的风险。

它还引发了其他问题，例如谁对机器人进行编程和控制以及目的是什么。 如果程序或数据被黑客入​​侵会发生什么？

孩子们能从机器人身上学到同理心吗？

教师处于备受信任的地位，负责弱势儿童和青少年的事务。 有立法框架和教师注册委员会来规范教师的专业行为，但它们并不适用于机器人。

教师有义务识别、保护和培养学生的最大利益。 这要求他们对个人的学习需求、行为和幸福感做出细致入微的判断。

这可能很难用固定规则、指令或机器人编程来捕捉。

正如研究人员指出的那样，如果儿童与模拟的而不是真正的关怀和同理心互动，这也会引发对儿童发展的担忧。

接下来怎么办？

明天我们的教室里不会有类人机器人。 但纽约的事态发展表明，它们可能成为未来的一个重要选择——尤其是在人们持续担心教师短缺和工作量的情况下。

如果我们要朝这个方向进一步前进，就需要回答一些棘手的问题。 我们需要教师在场，以确保机器人的使用方式能够在学生互动和学习时帮助和保护他们。
